## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. In a *parallel slopes* model with one numerical and one categorical predictor:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Each category gets its own slope and intercept</li>
  <li>Each category gets its own intercept but shares a common slope</li>
  <li>The numerical and categorical predictors are independent</li>
  <li>Only one regression line is fit</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Parallel slopes = same slope for all groups, different intercepts per category. Distinct from interaction models, where each group also gets its own slope.</div>
:::


## What you'll be able to do

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Distinguish between *population*, *sample*, and *sampling distribution*
- Use `rep_slice_sample()` from `moderndive` to simulate repeated samples from a population
- Describe how *sample size* affects the spread of a sampling distribution
- Connect the *Central Limit Theorem* to the shape of sampling distributions for the mean

::: {.predict}
Before we begin: which of these objectives feels least familiar to you right now? Hold that in mind — we'll check back at the end.
:::

Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. The *sampling distribution* of a statistic describes:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The values in a single sample</li>
  <li>The values in the population</li>
  <li>How the statistic varies across many possible samples of the same size</li>
  <li>How the population parameter varies across many possible populations</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> Sampling distributions are distributions of *statistics*, not of data. One dot on a sampling distribution corresponds to one summary statistic (e.g., $\bar{x}$) computed from one sample.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Sampling framework

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q2. As sample size $n$ increases, the standard error of the sample mean:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Increases</li>
  <li>Stays the same</li>
  <li>Decreases</li>
  <li>Is unrelated to sample size</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> Standard error of the mean = $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Larger samples → less variability in $\bar{x}$ → tighter sampling distribution.</div>
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q3. The Central Limit Theorem says:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>All distributions are normal</li>
  <li>The sample mean equals the population mean</li>
  <li>The sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal for large enough $n$, regardless of the population distribution's shape</li>
  <li>Larger samples have smaller means</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> That's why we can use normal-based methods for inference about means even when the underlying data isn't normal — *if* $n$ is large enough.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Second activity: chocolate-covered almonds

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. A population has a heavily right-skewed distribution. According to the Central Limit Theorem, the sampling distribution of the sample mean (for large $n$) is approximately:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Right-skewed too</li>
  <li>**Normal**</li>
  <li>Uniform</li>
  <li>Exponential</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> That's the surprising power of the CLT: regardless of the population shape, the *sampling distribution* of the mean approaches normal as $n$ grows. Skewness in the data does not imply skewness in the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$.</div>
:::

:::

## Check-in: The sampling distribution in other scenarios

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q5. You take 1000 samples of size 30 each, computing the mean of each. The histogram of those 1000 means is centered approximately at:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The first sample's mean</li>
  <li>**The population mean $\mu$**</li>
  <li>Zero</li>
  <li>The sample size 30</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> The expected value of the sample mean is the population mean. So the *center* of the sampling distribution = the parameter being estimated. (This is why $\bar{x}$ is called an *unbiased* estimator of $\mu$.)</div>
:::

## Check-in: Summary and final remarks

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q6. To **halve** the standard error of the sample mean, you need to:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Double the sample size</li>
  <li>**Quadruple the sample size**</li>
  <li>Halve the sample size</li>
  <li>Use a different formula</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> $\text{SE}_{\bar{x}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$. To halve SE, you need to *quadruple* $n$ (since $\sqrt{4n} = 2\sqrt{n}$). This is why bigger samples have rapidly diminishing returns on precision.</div>
:::
